brief.head: No rich autocracies
brief.text: Not one ad­vanced econ­omy is an au­thor­i­tar­ian coun­try[[x5]], Ajay Shah said. Rich na­tions share a pack­age: free speech, rule of law, great firms and fall­ing re­li­gios­ity. {057-C05}

brief.head: Pray for no windfall
brief.text: Ajay Shah prays that no wind­fall is ever found under the ground in India. A wind­fall brings wealth, he said, but not de­vel­op­ment, and not flour­ish­ing peo­ple. {057-C06}

brief.head: Fix the mosquitoes
brief.text: Development peo­ple con­fused pub­lic health with health care, Ajay Shah said. The state should fix water, san­i­ta­tion, air and mos­qui­toes, not build a hos­pi­tal in every vil­lage. {057-C14}

brief.head: Two halves, no talk
brief.text: Boys and girls in India don’t know how to talk to each other, Ajay Shah said. “Just imag­ine what a schism in the heart of the coun­try.” {057-C09}

brief.head: Clad the reactor
brief.text: Coercive power is poi­son[[x6]], Ajay Shah said, and must be clad like a nu­clear re­ac­tor. Every new power given to the state needs match­ing cladding. {057-C15}

thought.label: Thought for the day

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on the tenfold gap
lead.head: Mind the tenfold gap

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 57

play.label: Hear the case in six steps

body: Why is the av­er­age Indian’s out­put one-tenth of the av­er­age American’s, even after ad­just­ing for pur­chas­ing power? That, Ajay Shah said, is the sin­gle defin­ing ques­tion of de­vel­op­ment eco­nom­ics. {057-C01}
“It’s not 10 per­cent, it’s not 20 per­cent,” he said of the gap. “Ten X is a lot.”
The hosts recorded the episode on a moun­tain­top, with paraglid­ers leap­ing off nearby and, Shah joked, a hair light 150 mil­lion kilo­me­tres be­hind him: the sun.
Amit Varma asked for a sky-high view of the field. This was not about fis­cal deficits and in­fla­tion, he said, but “real lives, real peo­ple. This shit mat­ters.”
## Wrong model, wrong mood

Post-war think­ing, Shah said, drew its the­ory of de­vel­op­ment from Robert Solow’s growth model, in which out­put per per­son de­pends on cap­i­tal per per­son and on pro­duc­tiv­ity, then un­der­stood as ma­chines and man­u­als.
So poor coun­tries were told to save, build up cap­i­tal and im­port tech­nol­ogy. Development seemed as in­evitable as a puppy grow­ing into a dog. Foreign aid would merely speed it up.

India, Shah ar­gued, re­futes the model. Only about a third of work­ing-age Indians are em­ployed. Trillions of dol­lars sit in the global cap­i­tal mar­ket. An English-speaking elite can read any man­ual. If the model were right, India would al­ready be rich. {#richnow}
The wider record is worse. Of the coun­tries that were poor in 1945, he said, only South Korea, Taiwan, Israel and Chile have be­come rich. More than a hun­dred have not.
“So in fact fail­ure is the norm,” Shah said. “Success is the ex­cep­tion.” {057-C04}
Tell a climber that Everest needs only pro­tein bars, he said, and he will ap­proach it dif­fer­ently from one who is told the odds are against him.
## Fix the mid­dle

The data point one way. Lant Pritchett, the hosts’ friend, has found that me­dian in­come alone ex­plains 99 per cent of the vari­a­tion in poverty rates across coun­tries. Inequality, wel­fare pro­grammes and re­dis­tri­bu­tion add up to about 1 per cent.
“Ninety nine per­cent of the vari­ance of the poverty rate is ex­plained by growth,” Shah said, “not by the ob­ses­sions of peo­ple who are tak­ing in­ter­est in poverty di­rectly.” {057-C07}

Shah’s agenda has three pil­lars: firms as ca­pa­ble as America’s, a ca­pa­ble state, and a po­lit­i­cal sys­tem in which the state is the agent of the peo­ple. The rule of law, he said, is the raw ma­te­rial for the last two.

Behind all three stands so­ci­ety. In the World Values Survey, he said, 50 to 90 per cent of peo­ple in ad­vanced economies be­lieve peo­ple can gen­er­ally be trusted; in India the fig­ure is about 15 per cent.
## Under the lamp­post

Why did the field lose its way? Shah blamed three in­cen­tives: phi­lan­thropies hun­gry for credit, pop­ulist pol­i­tics that re­wards hand­outs, and eco­nom­ics jour­nals that prize rigour over im­por­tant ques­tions. {057-C17}
Varma, bor­row­ing Pritchett’s frame, called the re­sult kinky de­vel­op­ment: like a drunk search­ing for his keys under a lamp­post be­cause that is where the light is.
The cure, for Shah, starts in the mind. The dream of the book he wrote with Vijay Kelkar, he said, is that “the jour­ney to de­vel­op­ment is first and fore­most a jour­ney of ideas”.
Varma ended with a plea to think in­de­pen­dently and to judge poli­cies by their out­comes, not their in­ten­tions, the hosts’ own ar­gu­ments in­cluded.

second.label: Women and freedom
second.head: Breaking up, moving up
second.deck: Amit Varma recalls a column that drew heat, and what divorce rates reveal

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the divorce-rate column

body: When Ajay Shah sug­gested that a good in­di­ca­tor of so­cial progress is the rate of sin­gle moth­ers, Amit Varma of­fered one of his own. It had once got him a lot of heat.

In a con­tro­ver­sial col­umn, Varma had writ­ten that one of the great in­di­ca­tors of women’s em­pow­er­ment in India is a ris­ing di­vorce rate[[x2]]. More di­vorces, he said, mean women are being em­pow­ered to walk out of bad mar­riages. “Mostly that’s what it is.” {057-S08}

Shah’s other ex­am­ple was gay mar­riage, all over the ad­vanced world, he said. For Varma, an ad­vanced econ­omy is a full pack­age of free­dom[[x3]], not only a flour­ish­ing mar­ket­place: “free­dom of the mind”, “free­dom in the bed­room”, “free­dom in the pub­lic square”. {#freedom}

quote.text: I think the ris­ing di­vorce rate is fan­tas­tic be­cause it means women are being em­pow­ered to walk out of bad mar­riages.

third.head: Not for want of a manual

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on a show at the global frontier

body: On the ride up the moun­tain, Ajay Shah put a blunt ques­tion to Amit Varma. Was their own show, shot by Nomsita and Vaishnav on Sony equip­ment, in­fe­rior in any ob­vi­ous way to the global state of the art?

Varma saw no im­por­tant as­pect of their pro­duc­tion val­ues that fell short. Their mi­cro­phone, Shah re­ported him say­ing[[x4]], was lit­er­ally the global state of the art, with lit­tle left to im­prove. {#mic}

For Shah, that was the whole prob­lem in minia­ture. “We are bright enough to read these man­u­als,” he said. “We use these ca­pa­bil­i­ties to the hilt, then you’re at the global fron­tier. So then what went wrong?” {057-S04}
A tech­nol­ogy gap, he ar­gued, can­not ex­plain a ten­fold gap in in­comes. The an­swer has to lie else­where.

box.title: The ghost at Nehru’s table
box.text: Amit Varma wished that Lant Pritchett’s “dis­em­bod­ied spirit” from the fu­ture had sat in Nehru’s cab­i­net meet­ings. Pritchett’s data, that me­dian in­come ex­plains 99 per cent[[x7]] of poverty rates, an­chors the episode. Ajay Shah calls it “a very im­por­tant story”. {057-R02}

sections.label: The question
sections.head: Filthy lucre matters
sections.caption: the cost of being poor
body: Development eco­nom­ics, Ajay Shah said, be­gins with one ques­tion: why is India’s per capita GDP, ad­justed for pur­chas­ing power, one-tenth of America’s? Most coun­tries are poor, so India is only the guid­ing ex­am­ple. {057-C01}
The econ­o­mist Robert Lucas, in what Shah called “a beau­ti­ful paper” from 1988, wrote that once you start think­ing about this ques­tion, it is hard to think about any­thing else. {057-R11}

Shah ex­pected the charge of re­duc­tion­ism: is filthy lucre all that mat­ters? At Indian lev­els of in­come, he said, it is “an ab­so­lute cri­sis”. Children are stunted for want of pro­tein. In the North Indian win­ter, many can­not af­ford a hot water bath. “I know how mis­er­able I get if I am told not to get a hot water bath,” he said.
## A lux­ury be­lief

Amit Varma went fur­ther. The idea that money isn’t ev­ery­thing, he said, is a lux­ury be­lief[[x8]], one that elites hold in air-conditioned rooms and feel vir­tu­ous about while it hurts the poor. When one med­i­cal emer­gency can de­stroy you, money is no side issue. {057-C02}

~ Prosperity, for Shah, is about hav­ing choices. After Varma’s episode on cy­cling, he said, he “only walked away with envy at the ad­vanced com­mer­cial and or­gan­i­sa­tional cul­ture of Europe”. {057-S09} What peo­ple then do with their choices is their birthright.

quote.text: Money is a big freak­ing deal. The GDP num­ber is a big freak­ing deal.

sections.label: The old theory
sections.head: The capital mistake
sections.caption: the Solow model
body: Post-war de­vel­op­ment think­ing, Ajay Shah said, grew out of the growth model of Robert Solow[[x1]], the MIT econ­o­mist and Nobel lau­re­ate. Output per per­son de­pended on cap­i­tal per per­son and on pro­duc­tiv­ity, which was thought of as ma­chines. Hidden in­side, he said, was a the­ory of de­vel­op­ment. {057-J09}

The pre­scrip­tion fol­lowed: save, build up cap­i­tal, buy the right ma­chines, read the right man­u­als. The short­age was real. Before he first went abroad for his PhD, Shah said, he had never seen a high­way in India. {057-S01}
## Secret runes

UN bod­ies, UNIDO or UNCTAD, he could not re­mem­ber which, ob­sessed over “tech­nol­ogy trans­fer”, as if rich coun­tries guarded se­cret runes. His fa­ther told him this was com­pletely wrong. The knowl­edge was in books, pa­pers, man­u­als and patents, and “the bur­den is on us”. {057-S02}
Shah’s ver­dict on the old model was blunt. “The idea that pro­duc­tiv­ity is a man­ual, a doc­u­ment that can be trans­mit­ted beg­gars the imag­i­na­tion,” he said. {057-C03}
~ The old model as­sumed that India’s plen­ti­ful English speak­ers would bring the man­u­als in, and that would be that. “We are all Macaulay’s chil­dren,” Shah said. {057-J12}

quote.text: All the knowl­edge is there in the books, it’s there in the pa­pers, you buy the ma­chine, you get the man­ual

portraits.caption: Robert Solow
portraits.credit: Olaf Storbeck from Düsseldorf, Deutschland, CC BY-SA 2.0

sections.label: The record
sections.head: Not a puppy, a mountain
sections.caption: why failure is the norm
body: In the dawn of de­vel­op­ment there was a lot of op­ti­mism, Ajay Shah said. The very word sug­gested a child grow­ing into an adult, or a puppy into a dog: in­evitable, need­ing only calo­ries and pro­tein. Foreign aid and tech­nol­ogy trans­fer were the nu­tri­ents.
Amit Varma, the philoso­pher of the pair, ob­jected that a puppy grow­ing into a dog is “ac­tu­ally deeply tragic”. {057-J02}
The op­ti­mists were wrong. Of the coun­tries that were poor in 1945, Shah said, only four have be­come rich: South Korea, Taiwan, Israel and Chile. {#four}
## Respect the lad­der

More than a hun­dred did not, and in 2024, he said, no­body can say “just hang in there” any more. Failure is the norm. Yet the de­vel­op­ment com­mu­nity, he thought, still runs on “too much op­ti­mism”, the bet­ter to drum up money from donors. {057-C04}

His metaphor was Everest. Tell a climber it is just a mat­ter of eat­ing enough pro­tein bars, and he will ap­proach it dif­fer­ently. Tell him there is a high chance he will not make it, and he will train.
~ Varma called it a bril­liant metaphor. Climbing Everest is pos­si­ble, he said, and so is be­com­ing a de­vel­oped coun­try, with the right ap­proach.

quote.text: We will all do bet­ter by re­spect­ing the lad­der that we seek to climb.

sections.label: The first pillar
sections.head: Where GDP is made
sections.caption: the firm as the engine of growth
body: Output is made in firms[[x9]], Ajay Shah said, and that is the first grand pil­lar of de­vel­op­ment eco­nom­ics. Firms turn peo­ple, cap­i­tal, ma­chines, man­u­als and patents into out­put, and there is real magic in that. “If it was sim­ple, it would have hap­pened by now.” {057-C10}

What makes the United States great, he had said ear­lier, is not its gov­ern­ment but Google, Microsoft and JP Morgan. He urged read­ers not just to shop at IKEA but to walk around it and ad­mire the “au­dac­ity of con­cep­tion”. {057-R21}

Yet de­vel­op­ment eco­nom­ics ne­glects firms, Shah said, be­cause they are seen as rich peo­ple that fun­ders and jour­nals don’t care for. Studying them would re­veal the pol­icy fail­ures that hold them back. Firms and fi­nance, he said, are how India got to a three tril­lion dol­lar GDP. {#trillion}
## Seen and un­seen

Amit Varma saw a clas­sic case of the seen and the un­seen. What is seen is what firms have achieved; what is un­seen is what bad laws stopped them achiev­ing. Labour laws with the best of in­ten­tions, he said, crip­ple the growth of firms and so hurt work­ers. Everything the state does has a cost.
~ Varma also re­jected the trio of state, so­ci­ety and mar­ket. There are only two, he said: mar­kets are just how mem­bers of so­ci­ety do things for one an­other, vol­un­tar­ily. {057-C11}

quote.text: The first grand pil­lar of de­vel­op­ment eco­nom­ics is this cold state­ment that out­put is made in firms.

sections.label: The state
sections.head: Growth flatters the state
sections.caption: why growth can hide a failing state
body: Economic growth does not mean the state got bet­ter, Ajay Shah warned, though many Indians as­sume it must have. Development comes in spurts, and in a spurt the two can run in con­trary di­rec­tions. {057-C12}[[x10]]

The book *Building State Capability*, by Matt Andrews, Lant Pritchett and co-authors, mea­sured it care­fully, he said, and found that Indian state ca­pa­bil­ity got worse dur­ing the 1991-2011 boom. {057-R12}

Shah of­fered a con­jec­ture. As the econ­omy grows, big­ger sums are waved be­fore the same judges, reg­u­la­tors and of­fi­cials, and checks built for a smaller econ­omy break down. Good growth num­bers breed com­pla­cency, so the en­ergy to crit­i­cise the gov­ern­ment fades. Growth episodes, he said, con­tain the seeds of their own fall.
Amit Varma added that money flow­ing in turns the state into a beast that feeds it­self and gets bloated.
## The hare and the tor­toise

The UK and the US, Shah said, grew at 3 per cent for 200 years and never fal­tered. {#threepercent} Developing economies, by con­trast, have been more of a hare than a tor­toise, grow­ing in spurts. {#hare}

~ Shah cited a line he called beau­ti­ful, from John Maynard Keynes: the state’s job is not to do things a lit­tle bet­ter than pri­vate peo­ple, but to do what the pri­vate sec­tor will not do at all. {057-J17}

quote.text: So we should not make the mis­take of jump­ing to the con­clu­sion that be­cause GDP growth hap­pened, state ca­pa­bil­ity got bet­ter.

sections.label: The distortion
sections.head: Bright light, wrong place
sections.caption: the drunk and the lamppost
body: One frame from Lant Pritchett, Amit Varma said, made him see more clearly and also made him angry: na­tional de­vel­op­ment ver­sus kinky de­vel­op­ment[[x11]]. National de­vel­op­ment raises me­dian in­come, which is what gets peo­ple out of poverty. Kinky de­vel­op­ment zooms in on a nar­row prob­lem that can be solved and claimed.

Varma’s pic­ture was a drunk search­ing under a lamp­post[[x12]], helped by a po­lite Mumbai cop. Where did he drop his keys? A hun­dred me­tres away, in the dark bushes. Then why look here? “Because the light is here.” {057-J20}

Mainstream de­vel­op­ment eco­nom­ics does the same, Varma said, with RCTs on ridicu­lously triv­ial ques­tions, such as whether treated mos­quito nets help with malaria: easy wins for ca­reers. {057-C16}
## Three in­cen­tives

Ajay Shah blamed in­cen­tives. Philanthropists may be noble, but their staff need wins to claim, and con­sul­tants end up doing a joint secretary’s of­fice work. He imag­ined the boast: “I con­trib­uted to this pol­icy that got 73.4 peo­ple out of poverty.” {057-J06}
Populist pol­i­tics prefers say­ing “I gave you 2000 ru­pees” to cre­at­ing con­di­tions for growth, he said. {#rupees}
~ And in “the pe­cu­liar frat boy world of the eco­nom­ics jour­nals”, ref­er­ees ask for twenty changes and prize rigour over im­por­tant ques­tions. {057-J07}

quote.text: I feel that the en­tire field of main­stream de­vel­op­ment eco­nom­ics is doing that. They are search­ing for easy an­swers that don’t mat­ter.

Look around us in India today. Most peo­ple con­tinue to have a big state delu­sion. You go to the av­er­age pri­vate busi­ness per­son, how will you fix the coun­try? They want gov­ern­ment to do more, not less.

p3.title: Tales from the mountain
p3.deck: Four stories from the climb, and what each says about development

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on Taiwan, Korea and Israel
stories.head: Bad beginnings, rich endings
body: Since 1945, only four poor coun­tries have be­come rich: South Korea, Taiwan, Israel and Chile. Amit Varma called that “such a sober­ing and cau­tion­ary tale”, but also in­spir­ing: if they can do it, he said, so can we.
Ajay Shah wanted to dwell on how three of them began. “What a ter­ri­ble be­gin­ning for each of them,” he said.

Taiwan, he said, was an ir­rel­e­vant is­land off the coast of China that had en­dured a very cruel Japanese oc­cu­pa­tion. After the Chinese com­mu­nist rev­o­lu­tion, peo­ple flee­ing the main­land poured in. Their leader, Chiang Kai-shek, was no great per­son. “He’s no Nehru,” Shah said. “He’s a pretty rot­ten per­son in his own ways.”

Then Korea. The line be­tween North and South runs es­sen­tially at Seoul, and dur­ing the Korean War the city was taken and re­taken six times. {#seoul} With Second World War equip­ment, Shah said, Seoul should be thought of as de­stroyed on the scale of Berlin, Stalingrad or Dresden.
There are sto­ries, he added, of early South Korean gov­ern­ment of­fi­cials look­ing up to India and try­ing to learn from its civil ser­vice prac­tices.

And Israel. It fought a war in 1948, every step was a strug­gle, and it was sur­rounded by hos­tile states. “If you think fight­ing a two-front war is dif­fi­cult, think of what Israel has been through,” Shah said.
~ Yet some coun­tries placed under very ad­verse cir­cum­stances, he said, did man­age to claw their way out. {057-S05}

quote.text: So these things are very hard and they can be done.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the terrible starts of three success stories

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s happiest moment of recent months
stories.head: Denim at the cutting edge
body: One of Ajay Shah’s hap­pi­est mo­ments in re­cent months was a visit to a blue jeans fac­tory[[x13]] on the out­skirts of Bangalore. {057-S03}

The peo­ple run­ning it, he said, are in touch with the global state of the art. They know every ma­chine avail­able any­where. They care­fully work out the re­turn on each one and de­cide which ma­chine to adopt when.
Then they go to China, to Taiwan or to Europe, buy the ma­chines, read the man­u­als and de­ploy them in India. “There is no tech­ni­cal bar­rier,” Shah said.

~ That was the puz­zle. Labour is plen­ti­ful, cap­i­tal in the world mar­ket is “in­fi­nite”, and the man­u­als are read­able. If the old Solow model were true, Shah said, “by now India should have been a rich coun­try”.
stories.why: Knowledge is not what India lacks: its best firms can al­ready buy and run the world’s best ma­chines. Meanwhile about two-thirds of work­ing-age Indians are not work­ing, Shah said, and that is what de­vel­op­ment must ex­plain. {#employment}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the blue jeans factory

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah and Vijay Kelkar’s private brief
stories.head: A book for Nehru’s time machine
body: Economists, Ajay Shah said, are raised on the Solow model: pile on cap­i­tal, bring in ma­chines and man­u­als, and de­vel­op­ment should fol­low. Stepping out of it took him a very long time.
Slowly he came to state ca­pa­bil­ity, the rule of law, checks and bal­ances and pub­lic choice the­ory, “the cen­tral en­gine of think­ing about the mis­be­haviour of the state”.

He and Vijay Kelkar had worked in the Ministry of Finance. Writing *In Service of the Republic*[[x14]], their pri­vate brief was a ques­tion: which one book would they send in a time ma­chine to Jawaharlal Nehru? {057-S07}

~ Amit Varma spelt out the as­sump­tion: Nehru was a man of high in­tel­lect and great in­ten­tions. But pub­lic choice the­ory did not exist, Varma said, and Hayek was not taken that se­ri­ously, even though *The Road to Serfdom* was a best­seller.
stories.why: Policy fail­ure often re­flects the ideas avail­able at the time rather than bad in­ten­tions. That is why Shah calls the jour­ney to de­vel­op­ment “first and fore­most a jour­ney of ideas”. {057-C13}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the book for Nehru

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah reconstructs the mood of 1947
stories.head: All the world’s a war economy
body: To ex­plain India’s choice of a big state, Ajay Shah went into the minds of its founders, who weighed a UK-type strat­egy against a USSR-type one.

Russia had lost a war to Japan in 1905 and been whipped at Tannenberg in 1916, Shah said. {#tannenberg} Then the com­mu­nists kicked in the door, and a civil war ran till 1921. By 1945 it was the great­est land power in the world.

By the end of the Second World War, every major com­bat­ant ran a com­manded econ­omy, to vary­ing ex­tents: the USSR; Germany, where pri­vate firms worked at the Nazis’ call; a UK war econ­omy man­aged largely by John Maynard Keynes; and a US that passed a law to give or­ders to pri­vate firms.
~ Standing in 1945, Shah said, the il­lu­sion of the state on top[[x15]] was easy to slip into. {057-S06}

quote.text: So it was very easy to slip into a state on top il­lu­sion.

quiz.q: Of the countries poor in 1945, which four does Ajay Shah say have since become rich?
quiz.a: South Korea, Taiwan, Israel and Chile; more than a hun­dred oth­ers have not.

quiz.q: What share of cross-country variation in poverty rates does median income explain, in Lant Pritchett’s finding?
quiz.a: Ninety-nine per cent; in­equal­ity, wel­fare and re­dis­tri­bu­tion add up to about one per cent.

quiz.q: What did Ajay Shah’s father say about the old UN fixation on technology transfer?
quiz.a: That it was wrong: the knowl­edge is all in books, pa­pers, man­u­als and patents.

quiz.q: Besides shopping there, what does Ajay Shah urge readers to do at IKEA?
quiz.a: Walk around and ad­mire the com­pany: its de­sign, man­u­fac­tur­ing, stores and mar­ket­ing.

quiz.q: Why did Amit Varma once argue that a rising divorce rate is good news?
quiz.a: It means women are being em­pow­ered to walk out of bad mar­riages.

quiz.q: In Keynes’s line quoted by Shah, what is the job of the state?
quiz.a: To do the things the pri­vate sec­tor will not do at all.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 57. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Jawaharlal Nehru (Keystone View Company/FPG, public domain); Robert Lucas (Centro de Estudios Públicos, CC BY 3.0); Robert Solow (Olaf Storbeck from Düsseldorf, Deutschland, CC BY-SA 2.0); John Maynard Keynes (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); William Easterly (Jerry Bauer, CC BY-SA 4.0); Albert O. Hirschman (Sgt. Charles James, public domain); Daron Acemoğlu (MeJudice, CC BY 3.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon and Open Library.

shelf.title: In Service of the Republic
shelf.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ frame­work for Indian eco­nomic pol­icy: when the state should step in, why its fail­ures cut across every do­main (HR, con­tract­ing, bud­get­ing, checks on co­er­cive power), and why the fix is checks and bal­ances and small, re­versible steps.

shelf.title: Lant Pritchett Is on Team Prosperity (Episode 379 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Lant Pritchett
shelf.why: A deep con­ver­sa­tion with Lant Pritchett on why growth, not re­dis­tri­bu­tion, drives human wel­fare, why causal­ity runs from de­vel­op­ment to ed­u­ca­tion, and why many RCTs solve small mea­sur­able prob­lems in­stead of mov­ing the nee­dle on poverty.

shelf.title: Economic growth is enough and only economic growth is enough
shelf.creator: Lant Pritchett with Addison Lewis
shelf.why: Pritchett’s paper, which Amit calls a mas­ter­piece of data and clear lan­guage, finds that human wel­fare in­di­ca­tors from health on­wards cor­re­late at around 99% with per capita GDP, leav­ing re­dis­tri­bu­tion and wel­farism a sliver of the story.

shelf.title: National Development Delivers: And How! And How?
shelf.creator: Lant Pritchett
shelf.why: Amit says Pritchett’s pa­pers are eye-opening and sem­i­nal be­cause they are built on hard data and look at out­comes.

shelf.title: What I, as a development economist, have been actively “for”
shelf.creator: Lant Pritchett
shelf.why: Part of the body of work Amit wants every lis­tener to en­gage with di­rectly, not just through pod­cast con­ver­sa­tions.

shelf.title: Where Did Development Economics Go Wrong? (Ideas of India)
shelf.creator: Lant Pritchett and Shruti Rajagopalan
shelf.why: Amit calls Pritchett’s episodes with Shruti Rajagopalan ‘very good’.

shelf.title: Reforming Development Economics (Ideas of India)
shelf.creator: Lant Pritchett and Shruti Rajagopalan
shelf.why: A com­pan­ion to the ‘went wrong’ episode, for lis­ten­ers who want Pritchett’s case at length.

shelf.title: The Elusive Quest for Growth
shelf.creator: William Easterly
shelf.why: Easterly knocks out the fad­dish ideas that have dam­aged de­vel­op­ment and leaves you ask­ing what your the­ory of growth re­ally is.

shelf.title: The White Man’s Burden
shelf.creator: William Easterly
shelf.why: Easterly on why the West’s ef­forts to aid the rest have done so much ill and so lit­tle good: es­sen­tial read­ing on how in­cen­tives dis­tort de­vel­op­ment work, by a clear writer and great thinker.

shelf.title: The Tyranny of Experts
shelf.creator: William Easterly
shelf.why: Recommended along­side Easterly’s other books as es­sen­tial read­ing for un­der­stand­ing how the world of de­vel­op­ment re­ally works.

shelf.title: On the Mechanics of Economic Development
shelf.creator: Robert E Lucas
shelf.why: He calls it ‘a beau­ti­ful paper’.

shelf.title: Building State Capability
shelf.creator: Matt Andrews, Lant Pritchett and co-authors
shelf.why: It does care­ful mea­sure­ment of state ca­pa­bil­ity and finds that Indian state ca­pa­bil­ity got worse dur­ing the 1991-2011 boom.

shelf.title: Missing In Action
shelf.creator: Pranay Kotasthane & Raghu S Jaitley
shelf.why: A great book on the Indian state by friends of the show, worth read­ing even if, like Amit, you think mar­kets be­long in­side so­ci­ety rather than as a third pil­lar.

shelf.title: Rohini Nilekani Pays It Forward (Episode 317 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Rohini Nilekani
shelf.why: Rohini Nilekani’s frame­work of so­ci­ety, state and mar­kets as sep­a­rate pil­lars, which Amit cri­tiques: he sees mar­kets as a mech­a­nism through which so­ci­ety meets its own needs by vol­un­tary co­op­er­a­tion.

shelf.title: The Loneliness of the Indian Woman (Episode 259 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Shrayana Bhattacharya
shelf.why: Amit’s most pop­u­lar Seen and the Unseen episode, a con­ver­sa­tion with Shrayana Bhattacharya (who gave him the ‘anti-uncle’ label) on the eco­nomic and so­cial lives of Indian women.

shelf.title: The Loneliness of the Indian Man (Episode 303 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Nikhil Taneja
shelf.why: More than seven hours with Nikhil Taneja on the male side of the gen­der di­vide: half the coun­try can’t talk to the other half.

shelf.title: Demystifying GDP (Episode 130 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Rajeswari Sengupta
shelf.why: Rajeswari Sengupta on what GDP can and can­not mea­sure and how the num­ber is built, in­clud­ing how gov­ern­ment make-work and roads to nowhere in­flate it.

shelf.title: The Life and Times of the Indian Economy (Episode 387 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Rajeshwari Sengupta
shelf.why: A nearly ten-hour tour with Rajeswari Sengupta of India’s growth episodes and fail­ures and the costs of its post-independence eco­nomic choices.

shelf.title: We Should Celebrate Rising Divorce Rates (2008)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s provoca­tive ar­gu­ment that ris­ing di­vorce rates, often lamented as ‘be­com­ing like the West’, show more women gain­ing the agency and means to leave bad mar­riages.

shelf.title: Why Freedom Matters (Episode 10)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Despite the title, an eco­nomic his­tory of India told through the lens of free­dom: the boom after 1869, Nehru’s Fabian so­cial­ism, the lost years from the 1962 war to the Emergency, and the open­ing-up that lifted mil­lions out of poverty.

shelf.title: Walk around an IKEA and admire the company
shelf.why: He urges lis­ten­ers not just to shop there but to ad­mire ‘the au­dac­ity of conception’: how the fur­ni­ture is de­signed and man­u­fac­tured and how the stores and global mar­ket­ing are built.

shelf.title: The Poverty of Development Economics
shelf.creator: Deepak Lal
shelf.why: Further read­ing for any­one who wants to dig into the episode’s main theme of where de­vel­op­ment eco­nom­ics went astray.

shelf.title: Development Projects Observed
shelf.creator: Albert O Hirschman
shelf.why: Part of the hosts’ de­vel­op­ment read­ing list.

shelf.title: Gambling on Development
shelf.creator: Stefan Dercon
shelf.why: Part of the hosts’ read­ing list on why some coun­tries de­velop and most fail.

shelf.title: Why Nations Fail
shelf.creator: Daron Acemoglu and James A Robinson
shelf.why: Further read­ing on what sep­a­rates rich na­tions from poor ones, the episode’s cen­tral ques­tion.

shelf.title: The Narrow Corridor
shelf.creator: Daron Acemoglu and James A Robinson
shelf.why: Acemoglu and Robinson argue that lib­erty and pros­per­ity de­pend on a rare bal­ance be­tween state power and a so­ci­ety that pushes back, and that coun­tries can eas­ily fall out of that cor­ri­dor.

shelf.title: The Wealth of Nations
shelf.creator: Adam Smith
shelf.why: The found­ing text on how na­tions be­come pros­per­ous: Ajay says Smith is to eco­nom­ics what Darwin is to bi­ol­ogy, and it is ‘eerie’ how much he got right.

laughs.text: The episode is shot on a moun­tain­top. Amit calls the back­drop ‘the best green screen known to man. It is a nat­u­ral green screen.’ Ajay, the tech geek, shows off his hair light: ‘A hun­dred and fifty mil­lion kilo­me­ters be­hind me’, mean­ing the sun.

When Ajay com­pares de­vel­op­ment to a child grow­ing up or a puppy be­com­ing a dog, Amit cuts in: ‘The philoso­pher in me wants to argue with the econ­o­mist in you and say that growth from a child to an adult and from a puppy to a dog is ac­tu­ally deeply tragic.’

The ‘Bengali economist’ run­ning gag. Amit says: ‘be­tween us we are a Bengali econ­o­mist. We don’t like Bengali econ­o­mists. But be­tween us, like I’m Bengali, he’s an econ­o­mist.’ His proof of being Bengali: ‘I put on the jacket first.’ Earlier, Ajay men­tions that Amit has promised a YouTube short ex­plain­ing PPP ‘in English and in Bengali’.

Explaining why the lo­ca­tion changed, Amit says a leop­ard al­most at­tacked them and an­nounced, ‘I smell a Bengali econ­o­mist.’ He raised a fin­ger in reply: ‘No, you smell a Bengali and you smell an econ­o­mist.’ The real rea­son was that the light was fad­ing, so they watched the sun­set and fin­ished the next morn­ing, be­cause ‘de­vel­op­ment is a long jour­ney, so are episodes.’

Ajay on why at­tack­ing poverty di­rectly misses the point: it is like prim­i­tive peo­ple be­liev­ing ele­phant dung cures ele­phan­ti­a­sis be­cause the words sound alike, when the real cure is an­tibi­otics.
Mocking philanthropy’s hunger for credit, Ajay imag­ines a staffer’s ca­reer claim: ‘I con­trib­uted to this pol­icy that got 73.4 peo­ple out of poverty.’
Ajay on ‘the pe­cu­liar frat boy world of the eco­nom­ics journals’, where ref­er­ees join in as if they were co-authors, de­mand twenty changes, and the au­thor can’t say no.
Robert Solow, the MIT econ­o­mist and Nobel lau­re­ate, and the Solow-Swan growth model. Ajay calls it the hid­den ‘the­ory of development’ be­hind decades of cap­i­tal-first plan­ning.
‘We are all Macaulay’s children’: Ajay on India’s English-speaking elite, who were ex­pected to bring in the man­u­als that would make the coun­try rich.
Amit in­verts Tolstoy’s open­ing line of Anna Karenina (‘all happy fam­i­lies are alike’): poor coun­tries are poor in dif­fer­ent ways, but suc­cess­ful ones share a recog­nis­able pack­age.
The World Values Survey ques­tion ‘Do you be­lieve that peo­ple can gen­er­ally be trusted?’ Advanced economies score 50-90%; India scores about 15%.

Keynes on the role of the state: ‘the job of the state is not to do things a lit­tle bit bet­ter than what pri­vate peo­ple will do. The job of the state is to do the things that the pri­vate sec­tor will not do at all.’ Ajay re­grets not quot­ing it in their UPI episode.

The old line that every Nehru cab­i­net meet­ing had an empty chair for the ghost of Harold Laski, the Fabian so­cial­ist. Amit wishes the dis­em­bod­ied spirit of Lant Pritchett from the fu­ture had sat there in­stead.
The drunk look­ing for his keys under the lamp­post ‘be­cause the light is here’, re­told by Amit with a po­lite Mumbai cop, as a pic­ture of main­stream de­vel­op­ment eco­nom­ics.
‘A long arc from the French Revolution to Thomas Piketty’: Ajay’s short­hand for the en­dur­ing po­lit­i­cal ob­ses­sion with in­equal­ity.
